The Chevalley–Gras formula over global fields

Jianing Li Address: CAS Wu Wen-Tsun Key Laboratory of Mathematics, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, Anhui 230026, China Email address: lijn@ustc.edu.cn and Chia-Fu Yu Address:  Institute of Mathematics, Academia Sinica and NCTS
Astronomy Mathematics Building
No. 1, Roosevelt Rd. Sec. 4
Taipei, Taiwan, 10617 Email address: chiafu@math.sinica.edu.tw
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In this article we give an adelic proof of the Chevalley–Gras formula for global fields, which itself is a generalization of the ambiguous class number formula. The idea is to reduce the formula to the Hasse norm theorem and to the local and global reciprocity laws. We also give an adelic proof of the Chevalley–Gras formula for the class group of divisors of degree 00 in the function field case, which extends a result of Rosen.

Key words and phrases: 
class groups, ambiguous class number formulas, class field theory
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
11R29, 11R37, 11R34

1. Introduction

Let K/kK/k be a cyclic extension of number fields with Galois group GG. Let 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} be a modulus of kk, which gives rise to a modulus 𝔪K{\mathfrak{m}}_{K} of KK. The ray class group ClK𝔪K\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}}_{K} modulo 𝔪K{\mathfrak{m}}_{K} admits a GG-module structure. The Chevalley–Gras formula describes an explicit relationship between the generalized ambiguous ray class number |(ClK𝔪K/𝒞)G||(\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}}_{K}/{\mathcal{C}})^{G}| and |Clk𝔪/N(𝒞)||\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k}/{N(\mathcal{C})}|, where 𝒞⊂Cl𝔪KK\mathcal{C}\subset\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}}_{K} is any GG-submodule and NN is the norm map from KK to kk. In the case when the submodule 𝒞\mathcal{C} and the modulus 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} are trivial, the formula then relates the class numbers |ClKG||\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits_{K}^{G}| and |Clk||\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits_{k}|, which is the classical ambiguous class number formula due to Chevalley [8, p. 406]. A proof of Chevalley’s formula can be found in Gras’ book [12, Lemma 6.1.2 and Remark 6.2.3] or in Lang’s book [15, Chapter 13, §4, Lemma 4.1]. Lemmermeyer [16] gives an elementary proof which follows closely the approach taken by Lang, but avoiding the machinery of cohomologies. The existing proofs of Chevalley’s formula are reduced to a result of the Herbrand quotient of global units. In [10, Théorème 4.3], Gras gave a formula for narrow class groups with arbitrary 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In [11, Théorème 2.7] (also see the English translation [13, Section 2]), he proved this formula for ray class groups. His proof is based on Chevalley’s formula. Recently, a generalization of Chevalley’s class number formula to dihedral extensions has been investigated by Caputo and Nuccio [7].

In this article we give an adelic proof of the Chevalley–Gras formula over global fields. More precisely, using the adelic language, we reduce the formula to the Hasse norm theorem and to the local and global index theorems, which is shorter and more conceptual.

In the function field case, the class group of divisors of degree 00 deserves a special attention. The ambiguous class number formula (the case 𝒞=0\mathcal{C}=0) for functions fields was obtained by Rosen [19]. We also give an adelic proof of the formula with an arbitrary GG-submodule 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

In the last section we add an elementary exposition of a cohomological variant for SS-ray class groups, for the sake of completeness. This formulation is valid for an arbitrary Galois extension K/kK/k, and is essentially equivalent to Chevalley’s original formula in the cyclic case, thanks to the theorem on the Herbrand quotient of global units.

2. The Chevalley–Gras formula

In this section, we recall the definition of the SS-ray class group and prove the Chevalley–Gras formula. We then give some special cases of this formula for future convenience. In Example 2.6, we use this formula to reprove a classical result of Rédei on the 44-rank of the narrow class group of quadratic fields as this approach does not seem to appear in the literature.

2.1. Notation and SS-ray class groups

Let FF be a global field, that is, FF is either a number field (a finite extension of ℚ\mathbb{Q}) or a global function field (a finite extension of 𝔽p​(t)\mathbb{F}_{p}(t) for some prime pp). Let 𝒪w{\mathcal{O}}_{w} denote the ring of integers of FwF_{w} if ww is finite. The canonical embedding from FF to the completion FwF_{w} is also denoted by ww.

The letter SS always denotes a non-empty finite set of places of FF containing VF,∞V_{F,\infty}. Let K/kK/k be a finite Galois extension of global fields with Galois group GG. This question is answered mostly when K/kK/k is cyclic and remains open in general, even for the abelian case.

Suppose (S,𝔪)(S,{\mathfrak{m}}) is a pair for kk. Let SKS_{K} be the set of places of KK over SS and let 𝔪K:=𝔪K,∞⋅𝔪K,f{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}:={\mathfrak{m}}_{K,\infty}\cdot{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,f}, where 𝔪K,∞{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,\infty} is the set of real places of KK over the support of 𝔪∞{\mathfrak{m}}_{\infty} and 𝔪K,f:=𝔪f​𝒪K,S{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,f}:={\mathfrak{m}}_{f}{\mathcal{O}}_{K,S}. Then (SK,𝔪K)(S_{K},{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}) is a GG-invariant pair, and we say (SK,𝔪K)(S_{K},{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}) is induced by (S,𝔪)(S,{\mathfrak{m}}). In this case, we also write ClK,S𝔪\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S} for ClK,SK𝔪K\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}}_{K,S_{K}} and call it the SS-ray class group modulo 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}}. When 𝔪=1{\mathfrak{m}}=1, we write also ClK,S\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits_{K,S} for ClK,SK\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits_{K,S_{K}} and call it the SS-ideal class group of KK.

2.2. The main formula

Let K/kK/k be a cyclic extension of global fields with group G=⟨σ⟩G=\langle\sigma\rangle, where σ\sigma is a generator. Let N=NK/kN=N_{K/k} be the norm map from KK to kk. Let S⊃Vk,∞S\supset V_{k,\infty} be a finite non-empty set of places of kk and 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} an SS-modulus. Let Cl𝔪K,S:=Cl𝔪KK,SK\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}:=\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}}_{K,S_{K}} be the SS-ray class group modulo 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}}, where (SK,𝔪K)(S_{K},{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}) is the pair induced by (S,𝔪)(S,{\mathfrak{m}}).

For v∈Vk,fv\in V_{k,f}, denote by eve_{v} and fvf_{v} the ramification index and inertia degree of vv in K/kK/k respectively. In the number field case, if vv is real and every place w|vw|v of KK is complex, we say that vv is ramified in KK, and put ev=2e_{v}=2 and fv=1f_{v}=1, otherwise, we put ev=fv=1e_{v}=f_{v}=1. The following theorem which we call the Chevalley–Gras formula over global fields is proved by Gras in the number field case; see [13, Theorem 3.6].

Theorem 2.1.

Let K/kK/k be a cyclic extension of global fields with Galois group GG. Let 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} be a modulus of kk, and let S⊃Vk,∞S\supset V_{k,\infty} be a finite non-empty set of places of kk such that S∩S⁡(𝔪f)=∅S\cap S({\mathfrak{m}}_{f})=\emptyset. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a GG-submodule of the SS-ray class group ClK,S𝔪\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}. Let DD be any subgroup of IKS⁡(𝔪)I^{S({\mathfrak{m}})}_{K} such that the image of DD in ClK,S𝔪\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S} is equal to 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Then

|(Cl𝔪K,S/𝒞)G||Cl𝔪k,S/N(𝒞)|=∏v∈S∖S⁡(𝔪)evfv∏v∈S⁡(𝔪)[1+𝔪𝒪v:N(∏w|v(1+𝔪𝒪w))]∏v∉S∪S⁡(𝔪)ev[K:k][Λ:Λ∩N(K𝔪)].\frac{|(\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}/\mathcal{C})^{G}|}{|\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}/{N(\mathcal{C})}|}=\frac{\prod\limits_{v\in S\smallsetminus S({\mathfrak{m}})}e_{v}f_{v}\prod\limits_{v\in S({\mathfrak{m}})}[1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{v}:N(\prod\limits_{w\mid v}(1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{w}))]\prod\limits_{v\notin S\cup S({\mathfrak{m}})}e_{v}}{[K:k][\Lambda:\Lambda\cap N(K^{\mathfrak{m}})]}.

Here Λ={x∈k𝔪|(x)​𝒪k,S=N⁡(d)​𝒪k,S​ in ​IkS​ for some ​d∈D}\Lambda=\{x\in k^{\mathfrak{m}}|(x)\mathcal{O}_{k,S}=N(d){\mathcal{O}}_{k,S}\text{ in }I^{S}_{k}\text{ for some }d\in D\}.

To compute 𝔸k×/k×​N​(D~)\mathbb{A}^{\times}_{k}/{k^{\times}N(\widetilde{D})}, we consider the exact sequence

(2.4) 1→k×​N​(D~)​Uk,S𝔪/k×​N​(D~)→𝔸k×/k×​N​(D~)→𝔸k×/k×​Uk,S𝔪​N​(D~)→1.1\rightarrow k^{\times}N(\widetilde{D})U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}/k^{\times}N(\widetilde{D})\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{\times}_{k}/k^{\times}N(\widetilde{D})\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{\times}_{k}/k^{\times}U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}N(\widetilde{D})\rightarrow 1.

We claim that the last term is isomorphic to Clk,S𝔪/N(𝒞)\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}/N(\mathcal{C}). Hence

The first term of (2.4) can be computed by the exact sequence

Let GvG_{v} and IvI_{v} be the decomposition group and inertia group of vv respectively. For each place vv of kk, we choose a place ww of KK above vv. By local class field theory, H2​(Gv,Kw×)=kv×/NKw/kv​(Kw×)≅GvH^{2}(G_{v},K_{w}^{\times})=k^{\times}_{v}/{N_{K_{w}/{k_{v}}}(K^{\times}_{w})}\cong G_{v} and H2​(Gv,𝒪w×)=𝒪v×/NKw/kv​(𝒪w×)≅IvH^{2}(G_{v},\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{w})=\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{v}/{N_{K_{w}/k_{v}}(\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{w})}\cong I_{v}. Uk,S𝔪/N⁡(UK,S𝔪)≅H2​(G,UK,S𝔪)≅∏v∈S∖S⁡(𝔪)H2​(Gv,Kw×)×∏v∈S⁡(𝔪)H2​(Gv,1+𝔪​𝒪w)×∏v∉S⁡(𝔪)∪SH2​(Gv,𝒪w×)≅∏v∈S∖S⁡(𝔪)Gv×∏v∈S⁡(𝔪)1+𝔪​𝒪vNKw/kv​(1+𝔪​𝒪w)×∏v∉S∪S⁡(𝔪)Iv.\begin{split}U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}/N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S})&\cong H^{2}(G,U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S})\\ &\cong\prod_{v\in S\smallsetminus S({\mathfrak{m}})}H^{2}(G_{v},K^{\times}_{w})\times\prod_{v\in S({\mathfrak{m}})}H^{2}(G_{v},1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{w})\times\prod_{v\notin S({\mathfrak{m}})\cup S}H^{2}(G_{v},\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{w})\\ &\cong\prod_{v\in S\smallsetminus S({\mathfrak{m}})}G_{v}\times\prod_{v\in S({\mathfrak{m}})}\frac{1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{v}}{N_{K_{w}/{k_{v}}}(1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{w})}\times\prod_{v\notin S\cup S({\mathfrak{m}})}I_{v}.\end{split}

This contributes to the numerator of the right hand side term in the theorem. In order to prove the theorem, it suffices to show that the first term of (2.5) is isomorphic to Λ/Λ∩N⁡(K𝔪)\Lambda/\Lambda\cap N(K^{\mathfrak{m}}).

Recall that π\pi is the natural projection 𝔸K𝔪→IKS⁡(𝔪)\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}\rightarrow I^{S({\mathfrak{m}})}_{K}. Write D¯=π−1​(D)\bar{D}=\pi^{-1}(D) for simplicity. As Uk,S𝔪​N​(D¯)⊂𝔸k𝔪U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}N(\bar{D})\subset\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k}, it is direct to check that

(2.6) Λ=k𝔪∩Uk,S𝔪​N​(D¯)=k×∩Uk,S𝔪​N​(D¯).\Lambda=k^{\mathfrak{m}}\cap U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}N(\bar{D})=k^{\times}\cap U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}N(\bar{D}).

Given x=u​N​(d¯)∈Λx=uN(\bar{d})\in\Lambda with u∈Uk,S𝔪u\in U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S} and d¯∈D¯\bar{d}\in\bar{D}, we define a function ff as follows:

f:Λ⟶Uk,S𝔪∩k×​N​(D¯​UK,S𝔪)/N⁡(UK,S𝔪)x⟼umodN⁡(UK,S𝔪).\begin{split}f:\Lambda&\longrightarrow U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}\cap k^{\times}N(\bar{D}U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S})/N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S})\\ x&\longmapsto u\bmod N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S})\end{split}.

Suppose x=u​N​(d¯)=u′​N​(d′¯)∈Λx=uN(\bar{d})=u^{\prime}N(\bar{d^{\prime}})\in\Lambda with u,u′∈Uk,S𝔪u,u^{\prime}\in U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S} and d¯,d′¯∈D¯\bar{d},\bar{d^{\prime}}\in\bar{D}. It is clear that ff is a group homomorphism. We show that ff is surjective. Let u=t​N​(d¯​a)u=tN(\bar{d}a) be an element of Uk,S𝔪∩k×​N​(D¯​UK,S𝔪)U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}\cap k^{\times}N(\bar{D}U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}) with t∈k×,d¯∈D¯t\in k^{\times},\bar{d}\in\bar{D} and a∈UK,S𝔪a\in U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}. Then t=u​N​(a)−1​N​(d¯)−1t=uN(a)^{-1}N(\bar{d})^{-1} with u​N​(a)−1∈Uk,S𝔪,N​(d¯)−1∈N⁡(D¯)uN(a)^{-1}\in U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S},N(\bar{d})^{-1}\in N(\bar{D}). We have f⁡(t)=u​N​(a)−1modN⁡(UK,S𝔪)≡umodN⁡(UK,S𝔪)f(t)=uN(a)^{-1}\bmod N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S})\equiv u\bmod N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}). This proves the surjectivity.

The kernel of ff by definition coincides with Λ∩N⁡(UK,S𝔪​D¯)\Lambda\cap N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}\bar{D}). Lemma 2.3(3) shows that it also equals Λ∩N⁡(K𝔪)\Lambda\cap N(K^{\mathfrak{m}}). Thus, as desired, ff induces an isomorphism

(2.7) Λ/Λ∩N⁡(K𝔪)≅Uk,S𝔪∩k×​N​(D¯​UK,S𝔪)/N⁡(UK,S𝔪).\Lambda/\Lambda\cap N(K^{\mathfrak{m}})\cong U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}\cap k^{\times}N(\bar{D}U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S})/N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}).

Lemma 2.3.

We have the following equalities:

(1)(1) N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)∩Uk,S𝔪=N⁡(UK,S𝔪)N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})\cap U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}=N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S});

(2)(2) N⁡(K×)∩N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)=N⁡(K𝔪)N(K^{\times})\cap N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})=N(K^{\mathfrak{m}});

(3)(3) Λ∩N⁡(UK,S𝔪​D¯)=Λ∩N⁡(K𝔪)=Λ∩N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)\Lambda\cap N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}\bar{D})=\Lambda\cap N(K^{\mathfrak{m}})=\Lambda\cap N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}).

Proof.

Recall 𝔸K𝔪={(aw)w∈𝔸K×|aw∈1+𝔪𝒪w for each w∣𝔪}\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}=\{(a_{w})_{w}\in\mathbb{A}^{\times}_{K}|a_{w}\in 1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{w}\text{ for each }w\mid{\mathfrak{m}}\}. As mentioned, N⁡(∏w|vKw×)=NKw/kv​(Kw×)N(\prod_{w\mid v}K^{\times}_{w})=N_{K_{w}/k_{v}}(K^{\times}_{w}) for each ww as K/kK/k is Galois. For a place w∤𝔪w\nmid{\mathfrak{m}}, it is easy to see that NKw/kv​(Kw×)∩𝒪v×=NKw/kv​(𝒪w×)N_{K_{w}/k_{v}}(K^{\times}_{w})\cap\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{v}=N_{K_{w}/k_{v}}(\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{w}). We obtain N⁡(∏w|vKw×)∩𝒪v×=N⁡(∏w|v𝒪w×)N(\prod_{w\mid v}K^{\times}_{w})\cap\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{v}=N(\prod_{w\mid v}\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{w}). For a place w|𝔪w\mid{\mathfrak{m}}, we have the trivial equality NKw/kv​(1+𝔪​𝒪w)∩1+𝔪​𝒪v=NKw/kv​(1+𝔪​𝒪w)N_{K_{w}/k_{v}}(1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{w})\cap 1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{v}=N_{K_{w}/k_{v}}(1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{w}). It follows that N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)∩Uk,S𝔪=N⁡(UK,S𝔪)N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})\cap U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}=N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}). This proves (1).

To prove (2), let K××𝔸K𝔪K^{\times}\times\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K} denote the direct product of K×K^{\times} and 𝔸K𝔪\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}. Consider the exact commutative diagram

1→K×∩𝔸K𝔪→x↦(x,x)K××𝔸K𝔪→(a,b)↦a​b−1K×​𝔸K𝔪→1N↓N×N↓N↓1→N⁡(K×)∩N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)→x↦(x,x)N⁡(K×)×N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)→(a,b)↦a​b−1N⁡(K×)​N​(𝔸K𝔪)→1.\begin{CD}1@>{}>{}>K^{\times}\cap\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}@>{x\mapsto(x,x)}>{}>K^{\times}\times\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}@>{{(a,b)\mapsto ab^{-1}}}>{}>K^{\times}\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}@>{}>{}>1\\ @V{N}V{}V@V{N\times N}V{}V@V{N}V{}V\\ 1@>{}>{}>N(K^{\times})\cap N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})@>{x\mapsto(x,x)}>{}>N(K^{\times})\times N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})@>{(a,b)\mapsto ab^{-1}}>{}>N(K^{\times})N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})@>{}>{}>1.\\ \end{CD}

Note that K×∩𝔸K𝔪K^{\times}\cap\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K} by definition is K𝔪K^{\mathfrak{m}}. By the approximation theorem, K×​𝔸K𝔪=𝔸K×K^{\times}\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}=\mathbb{A}^{\times}_{K}. Since H1​(G,𝔸K×)=H1​(G,K×)=0H^{1}(G,\mathbb{A}^{\times}_{K})=H^{1}(G,K^{\times})=0 and GG is cyclic, the snake lemma gives an exact sequence

(K×)1−σ×(𝔸K𝔪∩(𝔸K×)1−σ)→(𝔸K×)1−σ→N⁡(K×)∩N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)/N⁡(K𝔪)→0.(K^{\times})^{1-\sigma}\times(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}\cap(\mathbb{A}^{\times}_{K})^{1-\sigma})\rightarrow(\mathbb{A}^{\times}_{K})^{1-\sigma}\rightarrow N(K^{\times})\cap N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})/{N(K^{\mathfrak{m}})}\rightarrow 0.

The first arrow is surjective by the weak approximation theorem. Thus the last term is 00. This proves (2).

(3) Hasse’s norm theorem says that k×∩N⁡(𝔸K×)=N⁡(K×)k^{\times}\cap N(\mathbb{A}^{\times}_{K})=N(K^{\times}). Recall that Λ=k×∩Uk,S𝔪​N​(D¯)\Lambda=k^{\times}\cap U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}N(\bar{D}) by (2.6). By (2), we have

Λ∩N⁡(UK,S𝔪​D¯)=k×∩N⁡(UK,S𝔪​D¯)⊂N⁡(K×)∩N⁡(UK,S𝔪​D¯)⊂N⁡(K×)∩N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)=N⁡(K𝔪).\Lambda\cap N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}\bar{D})=k^{\times}\cap N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}\bar{D})\subset N(K^{\times})\cap N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}\bar{D})\subset N(K^{\times})\cap N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})=N(K^{\mathfrak{m}}).

This proves the inclusion Λ∩N⁡(UK,S𝔪​D¯)⊂Λ∩N⁡(K𝔪)\Lambda\cap N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}\bar{D})\subset\Lambda\cap N(K^{\mathfrak{m}}). To show the other inclusion, note that Uk,S𝔪​N​(D¯)∩N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)=N⁡(UK,S𝔪​D¯)U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}N(\bar{D})\cap N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})=N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}\bar{D}) by (1). Then

Λ∩N⁡(K𝔪)⊂Λ∩N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)=k×∩N⁡(UK,S𝔪​D¯)=Λ∩N⁡(UK,S𝔪​D¯).\Lambda\cap N(K^{\mathfrak{m}})\subset\Lambda\cap N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})=k^{\times}\cap N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}\bar{D})=\Lambda\cap N(U^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}\bar{D}).

The last equality follows from (2.6).

The second equality in (3) follows from

Λ∩N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)⊂Λ∩N⁡(K×)∩N⁡(𝔸K𝔪)=Λ∩N⁡(K𝔪).\Lambda\cap N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})\subset\Lambda\cap N(K^{\times})\cap N(\mathbb{A}^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K})=\Lambda\cap N(K^{\mathfrak{m}}).

This completes the proof of the lemma.   

Remark 2.4.

The idea of our adelic proof of Theorem 2.1 comes from [21], which shows that Chevalley’s ambiguous class number formula follows immediately from the Hasse norm theorem, and the local and global norm index theorems. When the extension K/kK/k is abelian, we know that the analogous statements for the local and global norm index theorems hold true; see [14, Chap. IX, Sections 3 and 5]. However, to extend Chevalley’s formula to abelian extensions, the assumption that K/kK/k is cyclic is crucial in the argument used in [21].

2.3. Examples

We list some special cases of the Chevalley–Gras formula in the number field case.

Example 2.5.

(1)(1) If 𝔪=1{\mathfrak{m}}=1 and SS is the set of infinite places, then ClK,S𝔪\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S} is equal to ClK\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits_{K}, the class group of KK. The theorem says

|(ClK/𝒞)G||Clk/N(𝒞)|=∏v≤∞ev[K:k][Λ:Λ∩N(K×)].\frac{|(\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits_{K}/\mathcal{C})^{G}|}{|\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits_{k}/{N(\mathcal{C})}|}=\frac{\prod_{v\leq\infty}e_{v}}{[K:k][\Lambda:\Lambda\cap N(K^{\times})]}.

If we let 𝒞\mathcal{C} and DD be trivial, then Λ=𝒪k×\Lambda=\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{k}, the unit group of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}. The formula becomes the ambiguous class number formula for the class group

|(ClK)G||Clk|=∏v≤∞ev[K:k][𝒪×k:𝒪×k∩N(K×)].\frac{|(\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits_{K})^{G}|}{|\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits_{k}|}=\frac{\prod_{v\leq\infty}e_{v}}{[K:k][\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{k}:\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{k}\cap N(K^{\times})]}.

(2)(2) If 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} is the product of all the real places of kk and SS is the set of infinite places, then ClK,S𝔪\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S} is the narrow class group ClK+\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K} of KK. Similarly, Cl𝔪k,S=Cl+k\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}=\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{k}. Note that K𝔪K^{\mathfrak{m}} is equal to K+K^{+}, the group of totally positive elements of K×K^{\times}. For a real place vv of kk, [1+𝔪𝒪v:NKw/kv(1+𝔪𝒪w)]=[ℝ>0:ℝ>0]=1[1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{v}:N_{K_{w}/k_{v}}(1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{w})]=[\mathbb{R}_{>0}:\mathbb{R}_{>0}]=1. So the theorem says

(2.8) |(Cl+K/𝒞)G||Cl+k/N(𝒞)|=∏v∤∞ev[K:k][Λ:Λ∩N(K+)].\frac{|(\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}/\mathcal{C})^{G}|}{|\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{k}/{N(\mathcal{C})}|}=\frac{\prod_{v\nmid\infty}e_{v}}{[K:k][\Lambda:\Lambda\cap N(K^{+})]}.

If we further let 𝒞\mathcal{C} and DD be trivial, then Λ=(𝒪k×)+\Lambda=(\mathcal{O}^{\times}_{k})^{+}. The formula becomes the ambiguous class number formula for narrow class groups which is first proved by Chevalley in [8, p. 406].

We now use the formula (2.8) to reprove a classical result of Rédei.

Example 2.6 (44-rank of narrow class groups of quadratic fields).

Let KK be a quadratic number field with discriminant dd. Let T={p1,⋯,pt}T=\{p_{1},\cdots,p_{t}\} be the set of prime numbers ramified in KK. Let G=Gal(K/ℚ)=⟨σ⟩G=\mathop{\rm Gal}\nolimits(K/\mathbb{Q})=\langle\sigma\rangle. For a∈Cl+Ka\in\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}, NK/ℚ​(a)=a​aσ=1N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(a)=aa^{\sigma}=1 as ℚ\mathbb{Q} has class number 11. This implies that |ClK+[2]|:=|{a∈ClK+|a2=1}|=|(ClK+)G||\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[2]|:=|\{a\in\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}|a^{2}=1\}|=|(\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K})^{G}|. The latter term has cardinality 2t−12^{t-1} by Chevalley’s formula (2.8). In other words, the 22-rank of ClK+\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K} is t−1t-1. The following 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}-matrix is the Rédei matrix:

(2.9) R:=(log⁡(pi,d)pj)1≤i,j≤tR:=\left(\log(p_{i},d)_{p_{j}}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq t}

Here log:{±1}↠𝔽2\log:\{\pm 1\}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{F}_{2} is the logarithm map and (pi,d)pj(p_{i},d)_{p_{j}} is the quadratic Hilbert symbol of pip_{i} and dd at the prime pjp_{j}. Note that the sum of each row of this matrix is zero by the product formula of Hilbert symbols.

A theorem of Rédei [20, Theorem 3.1] says that 44-rank of ClK+\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K} is t−1−rank⁡(R)t-1-\mathrm{rank}(R).

The matrix RR is the transpose of the matrix in [20, Theorem 3.1]. One can check that the logarithm Hilbert symbol log⁡(pi,d)pj\log(p_{i},d)_{p_{j}} coincides with the logarithm Kronecker symbol (pj∗pi)∈𝔽2\left(\frac{p^{*}_{j}}{p_{i}}\right)\in\mathbb{F}_{2} when i≠ji\neq j. Here p∗=(−1)p−1/2​pip^{*}=(-1)^{{p-1}/2}p_{i} for pp is odd. If 2|d2\mid d, 2∗2^{*} is the number such that d=∏p|dp∗d=\prod_{p\mid d}p^{*}.

The proof in [20] uses the explicit construction of the 22-Hilbert class field. We give a proof by applying (2.8) to K/ℚK/\mathbb{Q}. By definition, the 44-rank of ClK+\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K} is rank4ClK+=dim𝔽2ClK+[4]/ClK+[2].\mathrm{rank}_{4}\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[4]/\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[2]. As we mentioned, aσ=a−1a^{\sigma}=a^{-1} for a∈Cl+Ka\in\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}. It follows that

amodClK+[2]∈(ClK+/ClK+[2])G⇔aσa−1=a−2∈ClK+[2]⇔a∈ClK+[4].a\bmod\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[2]\in(\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}/{\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[2]})^{G}\Leftrightarrow a^{\sigma}a^{-1}=a^{-2}\in\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[2]\Leftrightarrow a\in\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[4].

This gives ClK+[4]/ClK+[2]=(ClK+/ClK+[2])G\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[4]/\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[2]=(\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}/{\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[2]})^{G}. We now use (2.8) to compute the order of this group.

Take 𝒞=ClK+[2]\mathcal{C}=\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[2] in (2.8). It is well known that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is generated by the ramified prime ideals. We add a proof for this fact here for the sake of completeness. Suppose I∈IKI\in I_{K} such that its image cl⁡(I)\mathrm{cl}(I) is in ClK+[2]=(Cl+(K))G\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}_{K}[2]=(\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{+}(K))^{G}. Then Iσ​I−1I^{\sigma}I^{-1} is generated by some totally positive element α∈K×\alpha\in K^{\times}. Since N⁡(Iσ​I−1)=(1)N(I^{\sigma}I^{-1})=(1) in IℚI_{\mathbb{Q}}, we have N⁡(α)=±1N(\alpha)=\pm 1. 4. A cohomological variant for SS-ray class groups

Let K/kK/k be a finite Galois extension of global fields with Galois group GG. As in Section 2.1, we let 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} be a modulus of kk, and SS be a non-empty finite set of places of kk containing all archimedean places which is disjoint from the support of 𝔪f{\mathfrak{m}}_{f}. In this Section we shall discuss a cohomological variant of the ambiguous SS-ray class number formula of K/kK/k; see Theorem 4.1. This formulation has been generalized to an arbitrary algebraic torus TT over kk by Gonzalez-Aviles [9] when the modulus 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} is trivial, where the present formula may be viewed as the special case T=𝔾m,kT=\mathbb{G}_{m,k}. Furthermore, when K/kK/k is cyclic, we explain that Theorem 4.1 is essentially equivalent to Chevalley’s ambiguous class number formula (the case 𝒞=0{\mathcal{C}}=0 in Theorem 2.1), thanks to the theorem on the Herbrand quotient of global SS-units. The argument of the proof of Theorem 4.1 is slightly different from Lang’s exposition [15, Chapter XIII, Section 4].

We keep the notation of Section 2.1. Recall that we write ClK,S𝔪\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S} for ClK,SK𝔪K\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{{\mathfrak{m}}_{K}}_{K,S_{K}}. Let EK,S𝔪E^{{\mathfrak{m}}}_{K,S} be the intersection of the group of SS-units of KK with K𝔪K^{\mathfrak{m}}. We have the exact sequence

(4.1) 1→EK,S𝔪→K𝔪→iSPK𝔪,S→1.1\rightarrow E^{{\mathfrak{m}}}_{K,S}\rightarrow K^{\mathfrak{m}}\xrightarrow{i_{S}}P^{{\mathfrak{m}},S}_{K}\rightarrow 1.
Theorem 4.1.

Let K/kK/k be a finite Galois extension of global fields with Galois group GG. Let 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} be a modulus of kk, and let S⊃Vk,∞S\supset V_{k,\infty} be a finite non-empty set of places of kk such that S∩S⁡(𝔪f)=∅S\cap S({\mathfrak{m}}_{f})=\emptyset. Then

This completes the proof of Theorem 4.1.

Remark 4.4.

Suppose that K/kK/k is cyclic. We can identify H2​(G,M)H^{2}(G,M) with the Tate cohomology H^2​(G,M)≃H^0​(G,M)\widehat{H}^{2}(G,M)\simeq\widehat{H}^{0}(G,M) by periodicity for any GG-module MM. The theorem on the Herbrand quotient of global units says (see [14, Chapter IX, §4, Corollary 2])

(4.4) |H2​(G,EK,S)||H1​(G,EK,S)|=∏v∈S|Gv|[K:k].\frac{|H^{2}(G,E_{K,S})|}{|H^{1}(G,E_{K,S})|}=\frac{\prod_{v\in S}|G_{v}|}{[K:k]}.

Here GvG_{v} is the decomposition group of vv and EK,SE_{K,S} is the SS-units of KK. Note that EK,S𝔪E^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S} has finite index in EK,SE_{K,S}. So they have the same Herbrand quotient. Since H2​(G,EK,S𝔪)=Ek,S𝔪/N⁡(EK,S𝔪)H^{2}(G,E^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S})=E^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}/N(E^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S}) and H2​(G,K𝔪)=k𝔪/N⁡(K𝔪)H^{2}(G,K^{\mathfrak{m}})=k^{\mathfrak{m}}/N(K^{\mathfrak{m}}), we have

|Im ψ|=|Ek,S𝔪N(K𝔪)/N(K𝔪)|=[Ek,S𝔪:Ek,S𝔪∩N(K𝔪)].|\mathrm{Im}\text{ }\psi|=|E^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}N(K^{\mathfrak{m}})/N(K^{\mathfrak{m}})|=[E^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}:E^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}\cap N(K^{\mathfrak{m}})].

Thus, by Theorem 4.1 and Proposition 4.2, we obtain the ambiguous class number formula for SS-ray class groups

|(Cl𝔪K,S)G|Cl𝔪k,S|=∏v∈Sevfv⋅∏v∈S⁡(𝔪)[1+𝔪𝒪v:N(∏w|v(1+𝔪𝒪w))]⋅∏v∉S⁡(𝔪)∪Sev[K:k][E𝔪k,S:E𝔪k,S∩N(K𝔪)]\frac{|(\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{K,S})^{G}}{|\mathop{\rm Cl}\nolimits^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}|}=\frac{\prod\limits_{v\in S}e_{v}f_{v}\cdot\prod\limits_{v\in S({\mathfrak{m}})}[1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{v}:N(\prod\limits_{w\mid v}(1+{\mathfrak{m}}\mathcal{O}_{w}))]\cdot\prod\limits_{v\notin S({\mathfrak{m}})\cup S}e_{v}}{[K:k][E^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}:E^{\mathfrak{m}}_{k,S}\cap N(K^{\mathfrak{m}})]}

which is the formula in Theorem 2.1 when 𝒞=0\mathcal{C}=0.
